utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. And meanwhile I'll deal with a -- the following matter. On the 14th of March of 2014, the Chamber filed its decision on the trial sitting schedule instructing the Registry to arrange for the expert medical examination of the accused every four months, and to file the experts' reports. This medical report and regime was established in order to enable the Chamber to assess the impact of the trial sitting schedule on the accused's health. While there are a limited number of sitting days remaining, the Chamber maintains an interest in monitoring the accused's health albeit less frequently. In light of the foregoing, the Chamber hereby varies its 14th of March decision solely in relation to the frequency of the expert medical examination to once every six months as opposed to once every four months. Unless the Chamber hears further from the parties, this decision will take effect as of the 22nd of April, 2016.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll later ask you about the homework I asked to you do. I first give an opportunity to Mr. Ivetic to continue his examination-in-chief. And perhaps unnecessary I'd like to remind you as well that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, professor.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We left off dealing with Tomasica and I would like to again call up in e-court D1447, MFI, which will be your report as to Tomasica. And once we get there, I'd like to look at page 3 in English and page 4 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No -- I don't know, Mr. Ivetic, if you see anything on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do not. That's why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just black. Now there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I assumed as much. That's why I was waiting patiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'd like to look first at paragraph number 4 here in your report, and I would ask for you to please explain for us a little bit what your observations were in relation to this part of your Tomasica report and what is the significance of same.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Clark states in his report that there is a systemic list of main autopsy findings and other materials. That would mean that there is an also a systemic list of other autopsy reports and materials which are not main. It's not possible to explain anything in this way because there are markings in medicine which are used during the examination of mortal remains, and if they are well preserved, then there may be a special list as preserved body parts. If it is just one body part or bones, then another special group of mortal remains is made, and these body parts may later be joined to other body parts which are better preserved. If there are only bones, they are also marked in a special way and examined. So in this case, what follows from Dr. Clark's findings, he only examined the well-preserved bodies, those with fewer parts missing, which, in my view, should have been different. He should have examined the remaining bodily parts and bones as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could then move onto the next paragraph, paragraph 5 which is here at the bottom of the page in English and bleeds over onto the next page and here you have written: "It is noted that the mortuary facilities at Sekovaca were basic but that it was still possible to carry out a reasonably full and detailed examination in each case. Can bodies from mass graves of people who lost their lives in work conditions be fully examined without adequate equipment, as, for example, an X-ray machine or a fluoroscope?" First of all, professor, in your professional opinion, can bodies be subjected to a reasonably full and detailed examination without both an X-ray and a fluoroscope?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the X-ray machine and the fluoroscope have become part of the standard equipment for processing mortal remains, not only from mass graves but in the ordinary work as well, so practically -- all mortuaries and institutions that have forensic medicine well developed have such equipment. It's strange that in such a mass grave with so many mortal remains as this one, with the bodies being processed in peacetime, that the person who requested the examination of the bodies did not provide an X-ray machine or a fluoroscope and, in that way, reduced the possibility for the findings made during the autopsy to be all-encompassing and detailed and much more acceptable than the given finding.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can stay on this topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I can just ask a question. This sentence, you say, for example, an X-ray machine or a fluoroscope. Is it fact, in fact, that these two were not there? Dr. Clark says the place was basic, doesn't tell us exactly what it is that was available or not. You're giving examples of a fluoroscope and an X-ray and I'm asking you is it a fact, in fact, that there was no X-ray and there was no fluoroscope?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Clark mentions in detail in his report that there was no fluoroscope and no X-ray machine available. Let me just find the exact page reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In English, it would be page 5 under radiology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, dealing with the X-ray and fluoroscope equipment, how prevalent or how difficult to find are such devices in the region of the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's not difficult to obtain them as all because they were used during the processing of certain mass graves around Srebrenica, much earlier than the exhumation of the mass grave in Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And there are transportable or mobile versions of this equipment in existence and in use in the region?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are the so-called transportable X-rays which are used in operating theatres, and the military medical academy had some such machines in its possession while I was working there. They are movable and not stationary, not fixed. They can be moved because they have their wheels -- these are so-called transportable X-ray machines.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Earlier today you mentioned that the X-ray and the fluoroscope had become a standard part of the review of mortal remains. Could you briefly tell us what are the use and purpose of both an X-ray and fluoroscope in the process of performing forensic review of mortal remains?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes it's very difficult to find a projectile or metal body which caused the injuries in a person's dead body. That's why the best possible way to detect such metal bodies was resorted to and that is the use of those machines or equipment. The whole body is screened and that allows to detect any such bodies. Therefore, it is much more difficult for a pathologist could work without such equipment because then have you a can examine each body really in detail in order to find fragments of projectiles or mines and explosives that would indicate or explain the existence of injuries which are registered during the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated a few moments ago that X-rays and fluoroscopes were utilised during the processing of certain mass graves around Srebrenica much earlier than Tomasica. Which processing --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... are we talking about? Who was involved in that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look at the materials relating to Srebrenica, but the materials that I saw mentioned that the persons who processed the mortal remains around Srebrenica had at their disposal both an X-ray and a fluoroscope and that can be found in the relevant documents. I cannot point to exact portions, but I've read that and I can tell you that this was part of the procedure that was in place during the processing of mortal remains in grave-sites around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, may I put a question at this moment to the witness. Mr. Stankovic, you said a moment ago it's much more difficult for a pathologist to work without such equipment because then you have to -- you can examine each body really in detail in order to find fragments ... Have you any information how Dr. Clark and his colleagues worked? Did they do just that what you described as an alternative way to find the projectiles in a body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judging from Dr. Clark's report, they did not have an X-ray or a fluoroscope and they examined the mortal remains without those pieces of equipment. However, judging from the descriptions included in the reports of Dr. Clark as well as Dr. Durmisevic and Dr. Sarajlic, it does not follow that they examined the mortal remains in a more detailed way than usual. That also follows from the descriptions of the injuries that are included in their findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you explain the last part of your answer to Judge Fluegge's question, where you said that also follows from the description of the injuries included in the findings. What would you say about the description of the injuries that are included in their findings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The description of injuries in the autopsy reports is, to put it mildly, unacceptable from the point of view of forensic medicine because it provides few information that would allow conclusions to be made primarily about the trajectory of projectile through any given body. Fractures are mentioned but the fractures are described in such a way that, for example, that there are multiple fractures of the skull bones or that pieces are missing and that's the entire description and then a conclusion follows that the injuries were caused, for example, by the impact of projectiles fired from a hand-held gun. That' precisely why we have this situation. Last night I determined this once again when reading this document. For example, Dr. Clark says that an injury was caused by projectiles and Dr. Durmisevic, that it was caused by swinging a heavy, blunt mechanical weapon. So the question arises how one is to interpret such injuries if they are described in such a superficial way, that is to say, if in the autopsy report there is just one single sentence which is verified, which any of the people present may check for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, I'd like to look at item number 7 which we see here at the bottom of the page in English. It will be on page 5 in the Serbian of your report as to Tomasica. And I'd like to ask you what would be the normally accepted procedure for this aspect of the investigation; that is, describing the layout and the structure of the grave-site? What would be the normally accepted procedure in this type of forensic review?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the structure and the disposition of the grave is noted by the duty archaeologist. It is not usual for the forensic medical officer or doctor to enter such details, the disposition of the bodies in a grave and so on. But it is even more strange that Dr. Clark was not present when the grave was exhumed but then he did make a sketch of the exhumation on the basis of information that he received from some other people. It would have been logical for the head of investigations, that is to say, the prosecutor to have an archaeologist on the scene who would make such a sketch of the grave and the position of the bodies and everything else that archaeologists normally do in such situations, and for Dr. Clark to attach such a sketch and state that it was received from the investigating judge or the prosecutor who is in charge of the investigation in the given case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, in his report, I believe Dr. Clark, at page 2 in English and page 3 in Serbian talks about visiting the grave-site in December after all the bodies have been removed. From a medical and scientific standpoint what would be the purpose of such a visit to the work of Dr. Clark as a pathologist at that point in time when all the bodies are removed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any reason, but it's possible that he wanted to see the ground, to see if it was wet or if it was clay. In this particular case, it was an iron-ore mine, so probably that was his wish. But I don't think that in that part of the grave he would really get any important information from that. So I don't really understand why he wanted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is the presence of a pathologist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's just for the record I think my learned friend said it was on page 2 of the report. It is actually at the top of page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is hereby on the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, when -- are there instances when the presence of a pathologist is necessary at a grave-site during the exhumation process?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said yesterday that the presence of a court pathologist is obligatory at the beginning of the exhumation or, rather, the inspection of the ground where it is expected that the mass grave is to be found and then after a visit to the field he should also be there to notice everything that is important for a forensic medical officer. What were the bodies that were on the surface? Are there any differences with regards to the degree of putrefaction in between the bodies that were on the surface or deeper underground? Is there a difference in the material with which the mortal remains were covered? Is it stones or such was the case with ethnic Albanians in Bajina Basta who had been brought there in a refrigerator truck or whether the ground is without any hard substance such as stone and similar material. And then after that, he should also see how the bodies looked like while they were in the grave. So I think that forensic medical officer or a court pathologist should have been present all along during the exhumation in Tomasica which was not the case with Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And from the materials submitted by Dr. Clark, do you know if someone else was present during this time-period for the Tomasica exhumations; and, if so, whom?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for forensic medical specialist from Bosnia-Herzegovina in their autopsy reports, it's not noted that they were present during exhumation, that is to say, that they were present while the body that they were in charge of processing was still in the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, returning to your report as to the Tomasica material, I'd like to look at your questions raised in paragraph 8. You note that Dr. Clark says there may be a degree of misinformation. What problems do you see arising from this fact? What is the significance of this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any expert witness submitting materials to a Trial Chamber or the prosecutor or whoever requested an autopsy, has to describe in detail all the mistakes or errors and what he or she implies by an error, what is the degree of the error, and whether noting that there is an error may burden an autopsy report in any way. Dr. Clark's report does not include that, so it follows that the statement that there is a degree of error implies that the degree of error doesn't really exist. So it was necessary for Dr. Clark to explain in more detail what he implies by that and to point out to the Prosecutor, that is to say, the Trial Chamber, what that was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the next two paragraphs of your report, 9 and 10, found on page 4 in English, page 5 in the Serbian, you discuss the differing degree of preservation of the bodies that are reported by Dr. Clark for the Tomasica grave-site. And I want to ask you, first of all, what is your expert opinion as to the questions posed in paragraphs 9 and 10 and the percentages of 61 per cent preserved and 39 per cent exhibiting complete skeletonization?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's Dr. Clark's finding. I have no objections to it. There's nothing for me to dispute on the basis of what they did in the grave. He analysed the percentages and he stated the situation that was established. What is important is that this degree of decomposition of soft tissue in the bodies that were buried may point to a number of reasons that need be to explained. Namely, whether the death of the people who were buried in the mass grave occurred at more or less the same time; secondly, whether some of the bodies that were buried there were buried at different times, whether some mortal remains were buried at a later stage. Then it ought to be determined whether some bodies were out in the open, after death, and may have been attacked by insects or animals and damaged in that way. So, in my opinion, all these possibilities ought to have been explained in the report. Why such a difference among the bodies with 61 per cent of mostly preserved soft tissues and 39 per cent that were in the state of skeletonization.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From a forensic medical point of view, how drastic or benign is the difference in the preservation of the corpses that were moved from the Tomasica mass grave, the varying degree of preservation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you would need to know the post-mortem changes, specifically the complete skeletonization of the body out in the open, under the effect of insects. For this, two months are required. That's how long it takes for the body to be stripped down to the bone by insects and animals. At the same time, if the body is buried, then complete skeletonization would occur after a year, depending on the type of soil, is it clay or loose or sandy or rocky soil. So these would be -- these drastic differences may occur in one grave. It's possible for 61 bodies to be well-preserved and for 39 to be completely skeletonized. This is a phenomenon that Dr. Clark should have explained, as well as Dr. Durmisevic and Dr. Sarajlic. They should have done that for one simple reason. The preservation of body parts in this grave where we're talking about saponification for the most part, and this is a process of the transformations of fats when firm structures change into a runny substance that is similar to soap. And this phenomenon begins to occur after one or two months, then it's very pronounced after six months. After six months or longer, then this structure is turned into a kind of hard surface, and it resembles something like -- Well, therefore, after six months, we have pronounced changes of the soft tissues. They turn into a kind of sticky substance which resembles soap and this is why this process is called saponification. After a year or more, these soft tissues can harden, and they begin to resemble limestone or gypsum and that's how they're described. We have records of such changes and this is where we have this difference. Therefore, if there's an explanation stating that, for example, that bodies on the surface, which were on the surface of the grave disintegrated much faster compared to the other bodies, this is due to the putrefaction of soft tissue. Then we also have to say that we have a situation that if the bodies are marked in the order that they are exhumed from the grave, let's say the first body was on the surface, then the next ten bodies were also on the surface, then we have a specific situation that bodies of -- marked with high numbers, those that were exhumed last, are completely skeletonized, but in this explanation, that they were at a great depth and pressed by the other bodies and this is how -- this is the reason why soft tissue was preserved, this is something that cannot be concluded on the basis of the autopsy reports done by Dr. Durmisevic, Dr. Sarajlic and Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question. In paragraph 10 you say you're referring to the 61 per cent and 39 per cent and skeletonization. And you say: "Is it possible to claim that all the persons lost their lives at approximately the same time or not?" I can imagine that's a very interesting question. Does Dr. Clark or any of the other experts, do they claim to know whether they all died at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the information in Dr. Clark's report, we can conclude that they think that all the people lost their lives more or less at the same time and that there were no subsequent burials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where exactly -- because you say you can conclude. Does he state it anywhere, that they died more or less at the same time? Could you help me to understand where in the report I find that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to take time over the next break, then you're invited to do so. We -- it's not that I need an answer immediately. Yes? Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we look at item number 11 on the bottom of page 4 in the English, and at the bottom of page 5 in the Serbian, and here it said: "In his report, the forensic pathologist classified gun-shot injuries as definite, probable and possible gun-shot injuries, but he only counted definite and probable injuries in analysing overall findings. The question arises as to why gun-shot injuries have not been counted per each of the groups into which they were classified." Why, in your opinion, is this important.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe it's important because what is definitely established should be verified and it should represent a part of the table in which all these facts would be entered as definite and verified. There would be a second part of the table, with probable injuries which is not definite injuries. These injuries should be classified in this second column of the table with probable gun-shot wounds. There should be a third column with possible gun-shot wounds. In this case, in Dr. Clark's report, he added up definite and probable injuries, and on the basis of that, he did his analysis, counting the number of projectiles or injuries from ammunition on the bodies that he recorded. In my opinion, this is unacceptable. If something is definite, then it's definite. If it's probable, it's probable but it doesn't have to be so. If it's possible, it's possible but that doesn't necessarily have to be so. A more professional approach would be that he counted these injuries in the way he explained in the last section of the report. Based on this, it's very difficult to reach conclusions. On the basis of probable and definite injuries, he estimates the number of projectiles which caused the injuries and that's something that we would see later in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could turn to the next page in both versions of your Tomasica report. Paragraph 1 deals with X-ray and fluoroscope which we've also covered so I would like to move to paragraph 13. Here you say: "Why is the given analysis of post-mortem findings based entirely on the initial examinations, with no recognition of identifications subsequently established or body parts reassociated?" First of all, can you explain for us what are initial examinations in an autopsy and how the autopsy proceeds per normal practice after that point?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it says in Dr. Clark's reports, there were preserved body parts, there were preserved bodies, there were body parts that were exhumed separately where most of the actual body was missing, and then there were also bones. While working and during the DNA analysis and this you can see from the autopsy reports that were made by Durmisevic and Sarajlic, some of those body parts were identified and associated to the preserved body parts. The customary thing is that an autopsy is not complete until the moment when all the found body parts are given their first and last name associated with the proper person and only after that, the autopsy reports are collated which imply that these subsequently identified body parts are associated to the main, mostly preserved body parts. And in that way you have a complete analysis giving you the number of projectiles that the person was injured with and then also establishing whether there were any other injuries on the body, and that's when a complete autopsy, a final autopsy, is done, taking all of these factors into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a question at this point in time. I understand that you described a perfect procedure. But what -- what is -- has to be done if the pathologist doesn't know the name of the person? Should he ignore everything else he looked at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. An autopsy is not completed at the point in time when the corpse is examined. There are places where dead bodies are kept until the moment when it's possible to verify the identity of the bodily remains. The body is not buried until this identification is done, and is there -- the bodies are not handed over to the family until then. And during that period, the staff continues to work, providing descriptions of body parts. For example, you have a body with a missing right leg, and then analysing the reports. I happened to see that first there was a description of a body with a missing right leg. With a subsequent DNA analysis, it was established that the right leg belongs to a person that has been identified and then a report is made, and then that part of the body is associated to this part of the body that the leg belongs to. And only after that, the autopsy report is worked on further, adding this description of the state of the right leg, if there are any gun-shot wounds, any changes, any other injuries. This is then added to the original autopsy report, and then you make a new report with all these analysis and descriptions. So it's not necessary to wait with the actual autopsy. Work continues, but then when the analysis, such as the DNA analysis arrives, then the pathologist goes back to that autopsy and then associates that part of the body to the more preserved part of the body and then he drafts a supplement report and adds it to the original autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand from your answer you're describing an ideal situation. Thank you. Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, given what you know about the Tomasica investigations, were there any limitations that would prevent this procedure from being employed in the Tomasica investigation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The mass grave was processed in peacetime. There was enough time for the pathologist to process the bodies in this way and that way. If somebody were to ask me, did I work like this, if I worked in wartime conditions, then I would say that in wartime conditions we worked and we were exposed to artillery and projectile shooting. We had to work very quickly. And we would note that at the beginning of our report: Due to this, this, and that, we worked quickly on the autopsies. But in the specific case, there was enough time, there were enough staff, and enough resources to work at our own pace, and to apply all the well-known and accepted procedures in our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the method you've described for reassociations, based on the materials provided by Dr. Clark, was that adhered to in the Tomasica case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, or, rather, the people who were carrying out the exhumations, adhered to the method that all the body parts or complete bodies that were found were marked in the proper way, packed, and placed in one place, either a sheet or a bag or something like that. Therefore, as far as the registering of the bodies and the body parts from the grave was carried out according to the proper procedures, so this was not something that was placed into question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could now deal with -- I'll deal with paragraphs 14 and 16 in one group and I apologise, I'm going a little bit fast. I have a tendency to speed up and I'd ask, doctor that you also bear in mind also to try to speak more slowly so that our translators can keep up. In relation to paragraphs 14 and 16 of your report you posit some observations and questions as to the work on determining age ranges. First off, in the documentation that was provided for the autopsies relating to the Tomasica grave-site, did you, in fact, see the type of anthropological reporting or data that would be expected for such autopsy reports, as to age, sex, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the analysis that was carried out -- I can only see what I said -- well, let me just look at paragraph 16 to see what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It should be on the next page in the B/C/S on the screen.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the conclusion that in the table on page 8 of Dr. Clark's report in the Serbian, on the left side of the chart, we have age groups of persons under 20. There are groups. So persons under 20 and persons of 50-plus. Whereas, in the textual part of the report, it says that anthropological analyses verified that there were persons of 15 or under and 60-plus. So what is the actual situation? If that's the aim range, why does the table say that the age range is between 15 and 20 or persons of 60 and above? So this kind of conclusion is not acceptable because it does not arise from the actual table which I referred to on page 8 in the Serbian version. I don't know what page it is in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 14, you say that: "The question therefore arises is whether the persons who carried out the anthropological analysis were fully trained to perform the task that was entrusted to them." From the review of the autopsy reports, do we have information as to who performed the anthropological review?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of the documents, either in Dr. Clark's reports or the reports of the Bosnian forensic specialists provide the name of the anthropologist whose services they use. The autopsy findings of Dr. Durmisevic and Dr. Sarajlic do refer to an age estimate, but it says that they made that estimate. This can be concluded on the basis of the autopsy report. This was done by them and not by somebody else. We don't have the name of any anthropologists who worked on that mass grave. So as a forensic pathologist, I don't feel that I'm qualified to do the work of a forensic anthropologist, other than to note what is illogical in the types of conclusions that I already spoke about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What are the generally accepted standards for such information in autopsy reports? What is expected to be present as to the anthropological review?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forensic anthropologists describe the mortal remains, they describe the age, they determine the age group that the mortal remains belong to, and they determine if it's a male or a female body, or if it's a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do those reports typically indicate the identity of the person performing the review or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes. The autopsy report states the source of information used to determine the age. Dr. Durmisevic and Dr. Sarajlic did refer to the age groups, and they did that very properly by using the ID documents that were found in the clothing of the victims, but there are estimates of age that are stated without providing the source of information, in terms of whether it was they who made this determination or if it was somebody else. Based on the autopsy reports themselves, we can conclude that they themselves did that. Had somebody else given that estimate, they would be obliged to state that in their autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And moving away from Tomasica just for a brief instant, in relation to the autopsy reports from the ICTY exhumations in the Srebrenica area where Dr. Clark and other OTP experts worked, did those reports have the identities of those performing the anthropological review?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. One of the best known forensic anthropologist, Professor Harland, worked in the Srebrenica area. There were also others whose names were given. The people who had worked on these issues in the Srebrenica area. While I was working in Bosnia, specifically Sarajevo, I worked with international anthropologists. I think there was a person from Peru; I think her name was Eva. She was assisting me and I would refer to that in my reports. She helped me to determine the sex and the age of the mortal remains that we were examining.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Are there any additional observations that you feel you need to make in relation to items 15 and 16 of your report before we move on?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that everything has been covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I would move to item number 17 here on the same page in both versions. And here you state: "Any conclusion about the health of persons whose bodies were in a state of saponification, advanced putrefaction and skeletonization made without possession of their medical records or statements of health workers or family members, is unacceptable, and the question arises why Dr. Clark stated his view with regard to this." The first question I have for you is: Why in your expert opinion is it essential to have access to medical records as to the health of persons whose remains are being examined?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Autopsy reports of any victim or of any person in court proceedings such as this one, is something that is easily verified. So if somebody puts something in an autopsy report, they have to be very careful about what they will be asked, either by the Defence or by the Prosecution or by the Trial Chamber in a given court proceedings. So they should not refer to information that they did not themselves ascertain. In the specific case of Dr. Clark, there's a conclusion that these were healthy people. In one case, he found a catheter. In another case, he refers to finding a -- medicines in a pocket of the victim's clothing, and then in other cases, he comes to the conclusion that these were all healthy people. This type of procedure to get to a certain conclusion is not acceptable, it represents a professional error, and it is not something that can be applied for purposes of court proceedings such as this one, a court that was formed by one of the most important international bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we're just over the time for the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are. We take a break. And we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we'll resume at 8 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, before we continue, I think I asked you a question about where Dr. Clark claims that they were killed at the same time. Is it that you were referring to the preservation paragraph which starts with: "One of the most striking features of the Tomasica bodies was the degree of preservation, despite them reportedly having been in the ground for over 21 years." Is that what you refer to? Or is there something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I had the -- a different section in mind, and it's the report, the second paragraph from beginning, on page 1, where Dr. Clark says: "If, on the basis of unofficial conversation, I learned the people in the grave were mostly men who were mostly from a group of villages to the west of Prijedor were killed there in July 1992, and within several days, their bodies were moved to Tomasica and buried in a deep mass grave." That is the section. And another one, on page 3, the Tomasica grave, paragraph 2: "During exhumation it became clear that the bodies were grouped in various areas which, as believed was the consequence of the fact that they were laid there at different times." It's not specified at what times. So these were the two sections of the report that I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the first section you referred to doesn't contain any conclusion by Dr. Clark on the basis of his work but he just refers to what he was told. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. But in his report, he never mentions that later and does not explain the time of death of these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, he says something in his conclusions, I think, at the very last page of his report. He says: "What explains the difference in preservation," he says, "there was a preservation of many bodies" -- "the degree of preservation of many bodies was striking, despite having been in the ground for so many years." And the last line of that paragraph: "The reason for such variation is open to speculation." What he says: I don't know. And he deals with it by saying that he doesn't know. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. But I thought that perhaps he could have explained that in more detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if you don't know something, it's very difficult to explain, isn't it? I mean, you are requiring an explanation where someone says, I have no explanation which is perhaps not what you'd like to hear but -- and, of course, everyone would like to have an explanation, but if you don't know what that explanation would be, then I think it's proper to say: I don't know what the explanation is. And we all wished we had an explanation. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. But in this specific case, there are variations that would be more acceptable than just saying: I don't know. For example, why, in 60 per cent of the bodies found in Tomasica, those soft tissues were present and with 40 per cent they are absent. So on the basis of those findings - and Dr. Clark surely knows this - a possibility may be stated in order to avoid any dilemma. Then I would have nothing to ask here in front of this Tribunal, because Dr. Clark would have already explained that, and that was his obligation, inter alia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see what you're telling us. You're telling us that a possibility may be stated. If he would have done so, he might have been accused of speculation because a mere possibility is not a scientific finding, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But he could have provided explanation that I have given now, that before burial, the bodies may have been out in the open for a long time and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Insects and animals may have had an impact on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But what he says, that would be speculation, and I take it that -- of course, you can think of perhaps five or ten or a 100 possible explanations. But if you don't know, would you agree that from a scientific point of view, it's better to say: I don't know and if I wanted to invite him to give ten or 100 possible explanations, then you're asking something which he apparently considered not to be his task. That is, to speculate, on what possibly could have been the case. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Partly so and partly not. His duty is to explain why there is a difference with regard to the presence of soft tissues with 60 per cent of the bodies exhumed from Tomasica and absent in the 40 per cent of bodies. He has theoretical possibilities to give a theoretical explanation. It's not just assuming; it's a theoretical explanation on the basis of the available information and what he knows about decomposition of dead bodies over a certain period and under certain circumstances. So that's it. And if he said just, I don't know, I'm not disputing it. I'm not willing to go into it any further and dispute his finding. If he said he didn't know, all right, fine, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, sorry. I would like to take you back to paragraph 10 of your report. You put the question: Is it possible to claim that all the persons lost their lives at approximately the same time or not? That was the trigger appointed of the discussion we just had. Are you still claiming the same? And I would like to take you back to page 14 of today's transcript, line 2, you said: "From the information in Dr. Clark' report, we can conclude that they think that all the people lost their lives more or less at the same time and that there were no subsequent burials." Do you stand by that after we had just this discussion about Dr. Clark's report? Or would you like to change your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will accept Dr. Clark's statement in what Judge Orie said at the end. It follows that he actually says: I don't know. Because if he doesn't know why there is a different degree of putrefaction then he doesn't know whether all the deaths occurred at one and the same time. If that is so, I would then accept that fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He doesn't claim that they died all at the same time because that also triggered our discussion because in your report, you say: Can you claim? I asked you: Does Dr. Clark claim? And then you said: Yes, well, we could conclude that and from your answers until now, I've not heard any clear unambiguous claim by Dr. Clark that he could -- that he did conclude that all people died at the same time. From your sources mentioned, I conclude that that was what was reported to him and on which he takes no position. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 6 in the English and page 7 in the Serbian of your report, here at paragraph number 18, you discuss Dr. Clark's observations as to the multiple layers of clothing exhibited by some of the bodies from Tomasica, and just to refresh everyone's recollection on page 7 of Dr. Clark's Tomasica report in English, which is on the bottom of page 8 and the top of page 9 in the Serbian, Dr. Clark says: "Some had outdoor jackets and for some the amount of clothing appeared excessive, e.g. multiple upper layers, more than one pair of trousers, et cetera, but this was the exception and generally, the style of dress would fit with people who had died in the summer months." To you, what does this multiple layers of clothing indicate? Does it indicate people who had died in the summer months as Dr. Clark has --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Multiple layers of clothing are inappropriate for the hot months of the year. That's generally known and I see no reason why in July they would be wearing multiple layers of clothing so that was the basic question and the basic reason for the question. Multiple layers of clothing are worn, as is generally known, when the weather is cold and when one wants to protect the body from low temperatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you first of all, the transcript is not complete. Could you repeat exactly what you said in your question. Especially about to you what does the multiple layers of clothing indicate. You see that the transcript is not complete there. Could you repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I cannot repeat it verbatim since I was following this from the discussions that we had and it differed from my script.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You see what is missing and could you please -- I'll read to you what I have on my transcript. "To you what does this multiple layers of clothing indicate? Does it indicate people who had died in the summer months as Clark has --" and what then followed?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Stated, I think, stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we need perhaps an analysis of what Dr. Clark states and have a close reading. He said: "Some had outdoor jackets, and for some, the amount of clothing appeared excessive, e.g. multiple upper layers, more than one pair of trousers, et cetera, but this was the exception and generally the style of dress would fit with people who had died in the summer months. So I do understand what Dr. Clark says is that the multiple layers and a lot of clothing that was seen but that was the exception overall generally, people were dressed differently which would fit into dying in the summer. And I think, as a matter of fact, the way in which you phrased your question was the opposite of what I understand Dr. Clark to say here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I read the quote. Now I see that the quote I read is not in the transcript, so maybe that is the confusion here. But I read precisely the language the exact same way you did to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then it's about how you phrased your question. Your question was phrased suggesting that Dr. Clark claims that the multiple layers and the excessive clothing would demonstrate that people would have died in summer. And that's exactly what I am unable to read in what Dr. Clark says. And if need be, we could, of course, listen to the audio of your question to see whether -- because it's missing at this moment in the transcript and it will be worked over.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I thought I read the quotation and presented that to the witness, so I [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not the quotation that bothers me. It's the question you phrased that bothers me which, in my view distorts the meaning of the quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we can ask the witness how he understood, from a forensic point of view, Dr. Clark's findings as to clothing in the report that he reviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, most important is how we do read it and textual analysis of clothing and summer and winter is not within the specific expertise of a forensic pathologist. It's just ordinary language. And let me see. You said: "I read the quote" ... one second. I think as recorded, it certainly was not a quote literally read. It's something different. Some had outdoor jackets and for some the amount of clothing appeared excessive. But this was the exception and fit with people who were there, the whole thing about generally is taken out so it is not a literal quote, Mr. Ivetic, as it is recorded in the transcript. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My recollection is I read the quote verbatim, Your Honours. I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll verify that on the audio so it's important to have no doubts about this and that would then cover both the reading of your quote and the way in which you phrased your question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to your item number 19 which is on the page in both languages that we have on the screen, you talk of signs of burning on the clothing of some bodies. Now, first of all, have you in your career had any experience with review of bodies that showed evidence of exposure to burning?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have extensive experience, and I've written a paper of 24 pages which is in literature. It's about 24 carbonised bodies, the autopsy of which I performed in Siroka Kula, who perished in Gospic and the surrounding area in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then based upon that background could you explain for us the significance of what you're pointing out in relation to the Tomasica review and Dr. Clark's review of bodies that showed evidence of burning as highlighted in paragraph 19 of your report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that these are traces of burning on the clothes, not on the bodies, but on the clothes. Six persons are in question, and one may wonder where the bodies were and why the clothing burned. Perhaps they were in a building that was on fire or it may have been a consequence of the impact of mines or explosives. Or it may have been some other reason that fire caught some part of the clothes and caused the burning, but it indicates that the persons on whose clothing the traces of burning have been registered were in contact with flames.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to item number 20 of your report, and this is located on page 8 at the top in the Serbian version, you talk about Dr. Clark's conclusion that none of the clothing was of military type and that no one was carrying weapons. In your own career, have you ever found bodies in civilian clothing for which there was information from other sources indicating that they were potentially combatants?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of clothing, it's not possible to determine with certainty whether someone is a combatant or not and whether he or she participated in combat operations or not. Regardless of the clothes they wear, people may carry weapon, shoot, kill, or be killed. Therefore, it is no evidence whether these were military personnel or not. In July 1992, as far as I remember, members of the Muslim armed forces still had no uniforms. Most of them - this is my personal knowledge - wore civilian clothes. Those who lost their lives at Kula near Zvornik all wore civilian clothes so that does not indicated whether someone is a member of a military formations or not. Secondly, at the beginning of the war, the Muslims did not have sufficient amounts of weapons. In my practice, I never saw, including their mass graves around Srebrenica, that the dead were buried together with their weapons. I never saw that at any of the sites where I worked. And I think that the reports that I saw about the mass graves around Srebrenica that it never occurred there either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stankovic, can you direct our attention to Dr. Clark's report where he says these people were not combatants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me say again: The people may have been combatants or may not have been combatants. But in this specific case, it does not follow from Dr. Clark's report nor is it a part of his jurisdiction to establish whether they were combatants or not. Somebody else is to establish that; the one who is in charge of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did Dr. Clark establish that they were combatants or not? Where in his report can we find that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, if you allow me to find it during the next break, I may point to the exact portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just wanted to warn you, you should not criticise Dr. Clark for something which he didn't do. We had one example already and please be very careful in that respect and let us know after the next break where we can find that in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it page 7 in the English where Dr. Clark says: "Anticipating the assertion that these men may have been combat casualties, none of the clothing was of military type and no one was carrying any weapons."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is, indeed, totally different from what the witness claims in paragraph 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's why I was asking him if this was the section he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then let's be clear. If that's the paragraph you're referring to, Dr. Stankovic, Professor Stankovic, your task is not to tell us that we should not make any mistakes in drawing conclusions on what is factually described by Dr. Clark. If you comment on his report, then it should be the substance of the report, not on how we should read it. That's argument, and certainly Mr. Ivetic and the Prosecution will tell us what we could or what we could not conclude on the basis of Dr. Clark's report, together with all the other evidence we may have received on matters which are perhaps sometimes marginally touched upon in Dr. Clark's report. But you're invited not to comment on claims Dr. Clark did not make and he did not claim that he could determine whether the persons found in those graves were combatants, yes or no. He only explained here why he considered it relevant to pay attention to clothing of those persons which he then described in factual terms. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at item 20 Mr. Stankovic' report, the conclusions of Dr. Clark that he commenting upon that are quotation marks are precisely what I just read from Dr. Clark's report. He is very clearly and very accurately reporting Dr. Clark's conclusions in his report. I am at a loss now to understand what is going on in this courtroom, given that the passage I just read from Dr. Clark has been quoted with the exact words that are in the English translation in Dr. Stankovic's report, and now he's being criticised for commenting on those conclusions which are taken verbatim from the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are commenting on the answers Dr. Stankovic gave. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we look at item number 22 on the same page, you state as follows: "How is it possible that 'the clothing was often amazingly well preserved' and that just as many tears and other defects were present as to make confident identification of bullet damage very difficult and inconsistent."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we just move down a little bit so that we can see the footnote, what footnote 26 refers us to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Why do you raise this? What is the significance?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If something is well preserved such as clothing, then it is realistic to observe projectile damage made on the clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And ... and in relation to item number 23 of your observations as to Tomasica, which is on the same page in both languages, what would you provide to the answers that you pose in this paragraph based on your training and experience?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I already answered this question earlier today, that definite gun-shot wounds should not be counted together with possible gun-shot wounds in view of the fact that they do not represent the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I will deal with items 24 and 25 together, since I think they are related, so we'll have to go onto the next page in both versions at the appropriate point, but I'll read the full two paragraphs. In paragraph 24 you say: "If it is noted in the analysis that the bodies were exhumed 21 years after death, that they were in a state of saponification, advanced putrefaction or skeletonization, what is the basis for Dr. Clark's claims that, e.g., 88 persons were shot with one shot and 78 persons with two shots? " And then in 25 you say: "Based on what parameters is it claimed that only 709 shots were fired at the 293 persons, i.e., that the average was 2.5 shots per person?" And the question I have for you: Do you consider these conclusions by Dr. Clark as to the number of shots to be reliable in nature?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that Dr. Clark could have formulated it differently. He could have said: Due to lack of soft tissues and certain body parts on the corpses that were processed, 88 persons were shot with at least one projectile and 78 persons were shot with at least two projectiles, and then 25 -- actually 293 persons were hit with at least 709 projectiles and that on, average, 2.5 projectiles were fired per person in view of the fact that no one can say that the missing soft tissues and missing body parts did not also show signs of gun-shot wounds. So this is a conclusion that it is not possible to accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 26 of your report, you talk about the wearing of helmets and injuries to the -- gun-shot injuries to the head in relation to the same. I want to ask a more general question: In relation to the discussion of gun-shot wounds and their location, do you have any information as to the training typically given to soldiers in various armies as to what part of the enemy combatant's body should be targeted in the course of combat operations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I object to that question. I don't think it's within the expertise of Professor Stankovic to answer something like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you lay a specific foundation as to how he has gained factual information about what you asked him about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I thought I had yesterday, but let me try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stankovic, we looked at your CV yesterday and could you tell us during what period of time you were minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was minister of defence from November 2005 until May 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what was your rank within the military at the time that you were retired?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a medical Major-General of the Army of the Republic of Serbia and Montenegro, of the Army of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And during what time-period were you the director of the military medical institute?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the military medical academy, and I was the chief of the VMA, the top military medical institution, in the period from the 17th of January, 2002 until the 24th of April, 2005. Generally speaking, it's an institution with 1200 beds, 14 floors, 6.000 rooms, and 18 power stations, which provide the electricity to run the institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, during the course of all those positions that you held and your career in the medical field, did you have occasion to obtain knowledge of the training of soldiers in relation to targeting enemy combatants during combat?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And as part of the manufacture of military equipment during war, plans were made to produce helmets, bullet-proof jackets and so on, there were analyses carried out as to which body parts most often sustain injuries during combat between warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what were the results of that analysis as to what body parts most often sustain injuries during combat between warring parties?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two doctrines for armed conflict, two doctrines regarding injuries. The first one was that the enemy soldier should be shot in the area of the head or the left side of the chest because the brain and heart were located there, and shots to that part of body led to death and disqualification of that enemy soldier. The second doctrine was that wounding would be directed at the lower extremities or other parts of the bodies which do not lead to a quick death, i.e., which then require the engagement of another two soldiers in order to help the wounded troops and, in that way, one reduces the number of soldiers putting up resistance during a conflict between two warring sides. These two doctrines were developed in the department and accordingly the manufacture of helmets of body and bullet-proof jackets was planned --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down and repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, you have been asked to slow down and to please repeat what you just said as the translators require some assistance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you read where the interpreters had difficulties to follow him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, the last words we heard are as follows: "These two doctrines were developed in the department and accordingly the manufacture of helmets, of body and bullet-proof jackets was planned ..." And then we lost the rest of your words, and, therefore, could you please take up from there and continue.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that those parts of the body, or by hitting those parts of the body, soldiers would be killed or would very quickly lose consciousness and die and thereby the number of fighters in a conflict would be reduced, that is why special teams were worked to develop safety devices for those parts of body, including, I mean, helmets and bullet-proof vests. The second doctrine was to strike parts of the body that would lead to wounding and strong pain for the victims, such as lower extremities, possibly upper extremities, because in such situations, the wounded persons would be unable to move. They would be in substantial pain and would require other fighters in combat to assist them in taking the wounded out of the combat zone, thus reducing the number of fighters which could lead to the other side having a greater number of fighters. And then you would get the outcome of the battle that would be desired by one of the parties in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, we are hearing a lot about theories and what -- Could you tell us now exactly what in paragraph 26, what criticism, if there's any criticism in it, you are launching to Dr. Clark, or whether you are suggesting an explanation which, I then take it, you consider that Dr. Clark should have given it? Can you focus on paragraph 26. What are you claiming? Because the first part of the sentence is a question: Did he have information; and then the second part of 26, perhaps, but I'm not quite certain about that, that you're suggesting an explanation or -- what it exactly that you are doing in paragraph 26?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In analysing the number of projectiles which struck body parts, Dr. Clark analyses and indicates that the majority of gun-shot wounds were inflicted on the head or the chest. Those head injuries and chest wounds are parts of the body that are most often hit in combat by soldiers of the opposing side. This is the main question, i.e., the distribution of wounds on the bodies that were found on persons in the Tomasica mass grave, and that indicates that these injuries could have been inflicted during combat between two warring sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But Dr. Clark apparently refrains from describing possibilities. Sometimes he even uses the word "speculation" and just describes the facts he found. What's wrong with that from a scientific point of view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I already said that Dr. Clark did not establish the precise number of injuries to the head and the chest because the majority of the bodies that he examined were without soft tissue through which the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you've explained that. He's concluding possible gun-shots. He puts them aside and say: I only rely -- and we have heard your criticism about that. I only rely on what is definite or what is probable gun-shots. Fine. You have explained that. But just starting from there, what's then wrong with presenting it as he did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He comments the number of gun-shot wounds to the head and to the chest area and draws a conclusion on injuries to those parts of the bodies being the most frequent injuries that occurred, and that is why my finding and opinion, I said that this was a usual finding in all circumstances when we have combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you expected him to say therefore it must have been in combat? Is that how we have to understand your observation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm sorry, Your Honours, just give me a minute. I did not put this question to the Trial Chamber. I put this question to Dr. Clark, and you said earlier that I was asking you -- well, the best thing would be to have Dr. Clark in the courtroom so that we could examine this question together before you. This is something that we most frequently do in our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In courts in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Clark was here, and any question a party considered to be relevant could be put to Dr. Clark. But I do that understand in paragraph 26 you're not suggesting -- you're just putting a question to Dr. Clark without suggesting what the answer would be or should be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it would depend on Dr. Clark's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask one question. Is it also not possible that outside combat people who are being shot at could be shot at either through the head or through the left side of the trunk? What I'm trying to say is that kind of shooting does not only take place in combat. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree that you would observe those kind of wounds in the case of executions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we turn to the next page in the Serbian version to catch up with the English version of the report, I think we've already dealt with 29 and 30 which were related to the items we've just discussed. So then I would go to the next page in English to deal with your item 32 through 34. And here you are talking in reference to a table from Dr. Clark's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this point in time, I would ask for us to look at that table, which is P7443, and it will be on page 11 in the English and page 14 in the Serbian. And I think it should be Table number 6. And we'll just wait for the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With Table 6 in front of us, sir, I would ask you to elaborate and explain your observations in paragraphs 32 through 34 of the Tomasica report.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The table indicates that 45 of the total 246 shots were registered as shots to the back of the head which is 16 per cent of all shots fired at these 293 persons. Then there is 59 per cent of injuries to the trunk and arms, and legs, 4 per cent. Based on this information and in view of the way the conclusion was reached regarding 703 bullets, if I'm not mistaken, it's possible to conditionally accept the conclusions in view of the fact that you cannot be certain about the -- this kind of registered wounds from Tomasica because of the missing soft tissues. Also, another characteristic is that on the basis of this data, you could have drawn a conclusion about the position of the victim and the attacker, meaning whether the victim was turned away or facing the attacker at the time of death, which would then help to decide whether the injuries were sustained during execution or combat when one warring side was completely surrounded by the other side to the conflicts, and that is why there are the remarks made in my paragraphs from 30 to 36. I wouldn't deal with any other details unless there are questions about that. What is also very important here, if somebody was hit with a bullet to the back of the head, then the first thing that the forensics experts would observe would be that the wound was inflicted when the victim was in a submissive position. He was turned to the attacker with his back when he was attacked. Then we would analyse situations in which these injuries could take place. I think that Dr. Clark could have provided a kind of explanation which, in the specific case, he did not provide.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian experts undertaking the post-mortem autopsy reviews, did they provide any of the explanations that you just talked about that Dr. Clark did not provide?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian experts did provide certain opinions regarding certain cases. But like I said in my analysis, when I analysed the cases, there were instances when the Bosnian experts said that the entry wound was on the front of the head; whereas, Dr. Clark said that the entry wounds was on the back of the head, so I pointed to these inconsistencies in a small number of cases because I believed that if these cases existed, then the entire analysis could be brought into question and it would need to be repeated in order for it to be valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we're at the time for the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Ivetic. Witness, we take another break of 20 minutes, and we'd like to see you back at 10 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take the break and resume as announced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll use the time for something -- to put something on the record. On the 12th of April of this year, the Prosecution informed the Defence and the Chamber via e-mail of the expected scope of its rebuttal case and, on this basis, the Chamber informed the parties on that same day that they should expect to file their final trial briefs by the 1st of September of this year, and this communication is hereby put on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'd like to now return to your Tomasica report which we should call up in e-court as D1447, marked for identification, and I would ask for page 8 in the English and page 11 in the Serbian to be displayed with a focus on item number 35, which will be at the middle of the -- just under the middle of the page in English. In item number 35, you are focussing on intact bullets that were recovered from the remains. As a forensic medical expert, what does the presence of an intact bullet of this nature in a body tell you? What conclusions can be drawn?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If an intact bullet is found in a body, it means that during its trajectory the bullet did not pass through any hard surface or hit any bone inside the body. That seems to indicate that the projectile was fired from a distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And what part of that indicates that the projectile was fired from a distance? What is normally indicative of projectiles fired from a distance when found in bodies?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering that only 7.62-millimetre projectiles were described and that's the ammunition for semi-automatic or automatic rifles that has a great impact and penetrative power, it means that in case the injuries were inflicted from a short distance, point blank or several metres or a dozen metres, they would cause an entry and exit wound rather than the bullet being lodged in the soft tissue structures of a man. That indicates that the projectile was fired from a distance of at least several dozen metres, possibly even 100 or more metres, taking into account the penetrative power that such bullets have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could look at item number 36, the next item of your Tomasica report, I'd like to ask you to explain the meaning and significance of this paragraph, of what is raised in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a projectile with a great velocity of bullet caused certain injuries on the body, that is to say, the bones, it does not necessarily mean that bones will be always shattered. Whether the shattering of bone will occur or not depends primarily on the angle at which the projectile entered the victim's body. In my practice, I had a chance to see many entry and exit wounds to the head in which the bones were not shattered. After the passage of such a projectile, you only had the entry and the exit wounds, and there were line fractures spreading out from the entry or exit wound but no shattering of bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can move to item number 37 which is at the bottom of the page and then continues onto the next page in the Serbian and it is completely on the page in English. Here, you say: "The following conclusion: 'Two of the three women found in the grave (cases 227T and 230T) appeared to have been shot by a handgun, one with a single entrance wound above the left eye and the other with two entry wounds towards the back of the head' is unacceptable, as in such cases degrees of likelihood are used in the assessment of the condition in which these bodies were found, and so the question arises why in this specific case, this principle was not adhered to." Now, first of all, sir, in relation to Dr. Clark's reporting as to these two bodies, how would you describe the specificity and quality of opinions as expressed by Dr. Clark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Mladic speak at a volume which is inaudible for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure what you mean by -- what is meant by the term "looks" or "seems." Perhaps like at the beginning of this report, it could be said probable, possible, or certain, injuries that were registered in the heads of these women were possibly, probably or certainly inflicted by a handgun.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have find anything else of significance to discuss as to the findings as to the women that are discussed in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
