utterances.text: Moving along then to item number 38 which is at the bottom of the English of the page that we have now, and it is on page 12 in Serbian. You say: "In which cases is it possible to find portions of no less than six bullets in and around a skull, as noted in case of 317T." Now, before I ask you any additional questions about this, I'd like to actually look at this particular part of Dr. Clark's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So if we can have P7443 and it will be page 16, paragraph 5, in the Serbian; and page 13 in English, also the fifth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here in Dr. Clark's report, it says: "In one man, there were portions of no less than six bullets in and around his fragmented skull, probably from a burst of fire directed upwards through the left side of his jaw (371T). In most cases, however, far fewer were found - recovered either during the initial washing of the body where they presumably fell out as clothing was removed, or during the post-mortem examination itself when discovered still within the tissues." Now, that we've seen what you have highlighted and what Dr. Clark says, from the standpoint of an expert in forensic medicine, can you explain for us why this is significant; that is to say, why you posed the question that you did in paragraph 38 of your Tomasica report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I read this section of the report of Dr. Clark's, I found it very suspicious how it is possible that fragments of at least six bullets were found in a skull. It's practically impossible. However, I think that there was a confusion here, that Dr. Clark, if the translation is good, made an error, because when analysing the autopsy report 317T [as interpreted], after I provided this opinion, I noticed that the pathologist mentions one projectile fragmented into six fragments. So it was just one projectile with six fragments, which is possible, considering the bone that it hit. So, therefore, this section of Clark's report should perhaps be corrected, that it's not at least six bullets but at least six fragments of one projectile. Therefore, I would change my question. It follows from this that the autopsy report was wrongly or erroneously interpreted in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, you say that you -- it -- it's practically impossible to find six bullets in the skull. What makes that impossible? If six shots were shot into the skull, why would it be impossible to find fragments of six bullets in the skull?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For a very simple reason. During the entry of projectiles to the skull, destruction of soft tissues and bones would occur, and after that, the other projectiles would inflict entry and exit wounds, and because of that, after a burst of fire is shot to the head of a victim, it's impossible to find as many as six bullets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Even if each one of the bullets was hitting a different part of the skull?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear your answer. Could you please repeat yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even in such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the record, I think Professor Stankovic repeats the code 317T, but I think in Professor Clark's report, we see the code is, in fact, 371T, just to avoid confusion later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report reads 317T in the Serbian language version. And in English, it's 371T. However, in Serbian, the number is 317T.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The transcript doesn't say what the interpreter just said. You said the report says 371T in the Serbian language version. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think we can easily establish ourselves that the English version refers to 371T and the B/C/S version refers to 317T. So that there's a difference in the two versions. But I think there's no further confusion caused by it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can now return to your Tomasica report, D1447, marked for identification, and this time I think we should go to page 9 in e-court in English and page 12 in e-court in Serbian. And I'd like to look at item number 40. In item 40, you state: "If bullets fired from hand-held fire-arms from contact or close range leave more or less marked traces of gunpowder explosion on the surface of clothing, soft tissues or bones of the skull, is it possible that they disappear and cannot be registered, and if so, in which cases?" And I'd like to ask for you to explain or elucidate on this topic in relation to the Tomasica investigation and the materials you reviewed.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Projectiles fired from contact or close range, after firing depending on the distance of the muzzle of the hand-held fire-arm from the surface of clothing or the surface of the body leave traces of the gunpowder explosion in the form of unburned gunpowder residue, burns or grease on parts of clothing or tissue or bone. In this specific case, if bullets were fired from contact or close range in the preserved soft tissue structures unburned gunpowder residue may have been registered by scanning electronic microscopy [as interpreted] as parts of them remain in the soft tissue and with saponification would not have caused such drastic changes that it would not be possible to identify them by a specific procedure. Also, if a projectile was fired and there was greasing of the surface of bones or soft tissue structures, by the impurities and grease which the projectile contains on its surface then it's realistic to expect that these layers of grease cannot be destroyed unless being washed, but even then, it's quite difficult unless they are washed by a brush. If there was burning of bone then it is realistic to expect that traces of such burning would be identifiable on the entry wound especially if talking about skull bones and that's something that happened. After the body -- I mean, the boy I mentioned in my expert analysis, after four years, I managed to find burn residue traces on the skull bones which indicated that the projectile had been fired from a contact or close range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I ask the witness -- What does this exactly refer to in the report of Dr. Clark? I see some observations you are making. As a matter of fact, it is a question. How does it relate? Where do we find the link to -- in Dr. Clark's report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a part of the report that indicates the distance from which the projectiles were shot. It's page 17 of the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seems to be page 14 in the English. Now, can you tell us exactly how it is linked to what we read there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even though the pattern of gun-shot injuries on the back of the head might imply that the shots were fired from a close distance, on the basis of a pathologist's finding, that cannot be proved. That's the position of Dr. Clark under item 5. And I believe, judging by my experience, that if these injuries had been caused from a close range, the traces of gunpowder explosion that I mentioned - not all of them but some - could be identified and registered on the surface of the clothing, that is to say, the surface of the human body which is being examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say it is possible to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes, I say that it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if you don't find anything of the kind, then you still would not know whether -- then you still would not know whether it's either fired from close range and that the traces were not detected or that it was fired from a long distance where traces could not be detected. Is that well understood or did I miss something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then the -- in the autopsy report, I would only state: on the basis of the finding it is not possible to establish the distance from which the projectile was fired. Not just on the basis of the autopsy finding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But in both instances, you wouldn't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in both cases, it would not be known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we look at item number 41 in your Tomasica report, it will be on page -- oh, we're on that page already. It reads as follows: "Why does Dr. Clark claim that ' close inspection of wounds through hair is also never easy,' when this is a part of the body that is very accessible for any kind of inspection an analysis during autopsy." Professor, for those of us don't have experience of how autopsies are performed, can you explain to us why do you say that hairs and wounds in that region of the body are accessible for inspection during autopsy?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because everyone knows that the tissue of the skull, of the head, in which hair grows but there are persons who don't have hair, like myself, it's very easy to get the tissue, to take it off from -- remove it from the bones of the skull, and after that, have a very clear insight in the kinds of injuries existing not only on the bones, but also in the remaining tissue of the head which is very easy to analyse. Whether hair can be shaved and then you have a clean surface remaining or you look at the inside layer of the scalp tissue where hematoma may be detected, or it is more suffused with blood, or there are injuries in the form of crash wounds, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then I'd like to move to item number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you do, would such an inspection of an injury that is not on hair be equally accessible or would it be more accessible than the one on the head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Equally accessible as registering injuries located under hair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could move to item number 43 of your report - and we have to go to the next page in the Serbian on e-court - and in relation to this paragraph, can you explain for us what is the significance of the question you pose in relation to the cited text from Dr. Clark's report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By analysing the fact of the distance from which the projectiles were fired, if a hand-held fire-arm were to be placed against the clothing one of the effects would be the so-called effect of flame, which could be detected on the entry wounds, the damage to the textile fabric, some changes caused by burning, caused by flame. Such changes on clothing do not disappear by being in the ground. The evidence of that are changes to clothing in six cases in which Dr. Clark registered traces of burning. Therefore, if the injuries to the bodies were from contact -- caused from contact range, it is realistic to expect that flame damage would also be detected on the clothing. And in those specific cases, no such damage to the clothing was registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 44 of your report, you pose a question why there has been no harmonisation of views. I think that we have already covered this when we talked yesterday. Are we talking about the same thing we were talking about here yesterday, or is this something else that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Here I'm talking about the same thing that I talked about yesterday because the customary thing when the person conducting the examination, the investigating judge or the prosecutor, once they note differences between experts in the submitted material, differences in their opinion and findings, that person in charge would instruct them to harmonise their findings. If they're not able to harmonise their findings, then he would order a new investigation with new experts who would then provide their own opinion which would be acceptable for the trial proceedings that were being conducted. And the Trial Chamber would decide about the credibility of each of the findings. And, again, I apologise, as it was just said that I intended to give tasks to the Trial Chamber – I do not, in any way. I apologise if I left such an impression, I am using this opportunity to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I'd like to move onto number 46 which brings us to page 14 of the Serbian version and the next page in the English version. And here you say: "Based on what parameters does Dr. Clark conclude the following: 'From the nature of these unascertained cases there must be a strong likelihood that a number of the 12 did die from a gun-shot injury, but the evidence was not there to prove it.'" From the standpoint of a forensic medical expert, how would you categorise or respond to the use of these words by Dr. Clark in the performance of his duties as a forensic pathologist?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If 12 bodies, particularly referred to by Dr. Clark in his report on page 19, did not have any observable injuries, and Dr. Clark states the probability that they were possibly -- had sustained gun-shot wounds, it's very difficult. There's no possibility of drawing that conclusion. He could have said six bodies - or 12 bodies, I apologise - in an advanced state of putrefaction, so that for them the definite cause of death cannot be determined with certainty by autopsy alone. And it's a different matter whether then other people who lead the investigation could establish through other investigative actions the cause of death of those people, perhaps based on witness statements, or other factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in your last numbered item from your -- from the Tomasica report, paragraph 47, you pose a question: "Can the cause of death be determined with certainty for bodies in a state of saponification, advanced putrefaction or skeletonization, and if so, based on what parameters?" What would be your answer to this question posed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my findings, subject to the training that I underwent, i.e. the forensic medicine school that I graduated from and that was recognised in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, my conclusion would be that a corpse in an advanced state of putrefaction or skeletonization is one for which cause of death cannot definitely be established. If there are entry-exit gun-shot wounds observed in the head, I would note these injuries and perhaps other injuries, but then again, I would say that the person conducting the investigation would need to use other types of evidence, such as witness statements or other types of evidence to qualify the cause of death of that person later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I ask one question. Do I understand you well that Dr. Clark should have started interviewing witnesses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Dr. Clark is in the Prosecutor's team and the Prosecutor is in charge of the investigation. So Dr. Clark can tell the Prosecutor only as much as he is able to tell him and the Prosecutor is the one who subsequently, in view of the observed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, do you know whether the Prosecution did this or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on the information in the case file, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which case file?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ones that were available to me, and that's the report of Dr. Clark, the autopsy report, a summary of the autopsy reports of Dr. Clark, autopsy reports that were drafted by Drs. Durmisevic and Sarajlic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What you're telling us the forensic pathologist did not take such action. At the same time, you tell me that you didn't expect Dr. Clark to do that. But what the Prosecution did, do you have any knowledge about that? What witnesses they interviewed, what evidence they presented in court, what DNA analysis was presented here? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have any detailed information about that. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because I'm a bit confused. What I understand you're telling us is that if you establish what you have established in this report, you should do other things to establish what happened. Now, that is not the same as saying Dr. Clark did right or wrong. I thought you were commenting on Dr. Clark's report; but what you're telling us now is what others should do on the basis of sometimes the lack of findings by Dr. Clark. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am commenting on the fact that the cause of death that -- what I'm saying is that Dr. Clark gave his comments on causes of death and then he said in his findings that death was caused as a consequence of gun-shot wounds to the heads. I'm not disputing that. What I'm looking at is the way we come to such conclusions. I'm not disputing what Dr. Clark said. All I said was that the best way to formulate that is to say that the corpse was in a state of advanced decomposition that such-and-such wounds were observed on the head. It's possible that the causes of death is in a casual relationship to those wounding but as to whether the actual cause of death is due to gun-shot wounds would something that would be in the remit of the Prosecutor. That is not something that is in this material. And it shouldn't be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I understand that you do not disagree, apart from how he formulated it, and that perhaps he should have suggested to give it any follow-up from others. But you do not contest what he finds and what he concludes but others should give it a follow-up. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But all that has to be there is to say that the corpse is in an advance state of decomposition and that one should not determine the cause and origin of death with any certainty. Other than that, everything else is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To follow up on the Judge's question, I want to go back to your paragraph 46, which, again, is dealing exactly with what Dr. Clark did in, in fact, say. So we're talking about what Dr. Clark did, in fact, say. And for these bodies, were these bodies, as described by Clark in an advanced state of putrefaction?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just need to look at page 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you give us the English page, Mr. Ivetic. That would certainly assist me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbian, it's page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the English, that will be on page 15. Yes, bottom of page 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of Dr. Clark's report?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Of Dr. Clark's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have it on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So that's P7443. Page 15 at the bottom on English. And if we could have page 18 of the same in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you may, in this table, you can see a case where we have 013E on the left side and then comments, for example, for case 013E Clark says: "Third female victim, only post-mortem injuries visible." And then after that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let me just correct you, it's 013T.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't think we've got a translation of the last part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what you last said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying that on the left side -- actually looking, it's on the right side but looking from my left side we have the case numbers. In the middle, we have the comments. And then after this table there is Dr. Clark's general commentary to which I am objecting. It says: "013T, the third of the women victims; apparent post-mortem injuries only." Meaning injuries sustained after death. And then we have: "169T, gun-shot injury of shoulder not considered necessarily fatal but also head missing." "194T, apparent bullet hole in shirt."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, the translators are having difficulty keeping up with you. Could you please repeat the last number that you gave. The last part that we heard the gun-shot injury of the shoulder not considered necessarily fatal but also head missing. If you could please take up your answer from that point, and please try to slow down in the manner of speech so that the translators can adequately follow what you are telling us.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "122, no gun-shot injuries in parts present but head missing. After that, "136T, no gun-shot injuries. Although blunt force trauma to skull, not clear whether before or after death." And so on. I can read all of it, but on the basis of these descriptions and on the basis of such sketchy data, Dr. Clark allows for the possibility that there were gun-shot wounds. I'm not disputing that fact, but you cannot draw conclusions on the basis of assumptions. This is completely without basis, and it's unacceptable from a forensic medical point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But what conclusions does he draw from that? You say it's possible that they died from bullet injuries. Does ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In his findings below the table, Dr. Clark states - I'm reading: "From the nature of these unascertained cases there must be a strong likelihood that a number of the 12 did die from a gun-shot injury, but the evidence was not there to prove it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand this to be that he cannot draw any conclusions apart that he considers it likely that some of them may have died from bullet wounds but he refrains and says cause of death is unascertained. From what I understand, you agree with him on that final conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with the final conclusions but I don't agree with the manner in which the conclusion was made. Because it is not usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can now return to your report, and it's D1477 MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can -- I apologise. I lost my page number. If we can look at -- I believe it's part B of your report where you talk about various cases that you selected - one moment please - yes. And the heading is: "Some of the cases in which inconsistency has been observed between the autopsy reports of Dr. Clark and the pathologists commissioned by the prosecutor of Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Page 10 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 10 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's also the right time to inquire about what the witness may have found out overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you like me to do it? Then, Mr. Stankovic, have you found any other cases of inconsistencies; and how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you gave me the assignment to find ten. I found ten. I could have gone on. To tell the truth, I was tired, so I couldn't continue with the work. But we have case 051T, Redzep Karupovic [phoen], the difference -- well, it's just one detail. Gun-shot wounds, according to Dr. Durmisevic, in the area of the ribs and the right pelvic bone which he indicated to be gun-shot wounds, according to Dr. Clark, are considered to be post-mortem injuries. Then Dr. Durmisevic cannot ascertain what was the cause of the injury in the left lower jaw. However, Dr. Clark believes that it's a gun-shot wound. Then 081T, the autopsy report for Fekir Kadiric [phoen]. There is a difference. Dr. Durmisevic looks at a fracture on the left side of the skull. Dr. Clark claims that this injury was a gun-shot injury. Dr. Durmisevic explained that the left rib area injury was caused by projectiles; whereas, Dr. Clark believes that these were injuries of the ribs which were sustained post-mortem. 108T, Hasan Kamenac [phoen]. According to Dr. Durmisevic, the injuries were inflicted by at least two projectiles, whereas, according to doctor projectiles [as interpreted], it was at least one projectile. Dr. Clark did not describe the fractures at all of the first and second joint, whereas, Dr. Durmisevic did describe those injuries. Case 157T, it's an unknown person. What are the differences? Dr. Sarajlic allows for the possibilities that both gun-shots were caused by one projectile, whereas Dr. Clark states that the injuries were inflicted by at least two projectiles. Case 220T, an unidentified person. The inconsistency lies with a number of projectiles that caused the gun-shot injuries and in the possible mechanism of inflicting two gun-shot wounds by one projectile. Case 380T, Smajl Zahirovic [phoen]. Dr. Nermin Sarajlic states that there is a minimum of three projectiles and assumes on page 3 that the fragmentation of the skull bones indicates the action of a projectile but that this was not possible to prove with any certainty. Dr. Clark believes there were at least four hits. Case 399T. I'm talking about the autopsy. It's an unidentified person. Dr. Sarajlic does not rule out the possibility that there was more than one gun-shot wound to the head, whereas Dr. Clark rules out that possibility. Dr. Clark describes the possibility of gun-shot injuries of the left elbow, whereas, Sarajlic talks about the right thumb bone. I think he probably thinks of -- is thinking of the radius which was fractured by a blunt mechanical force. So in one case it could be a gun-shot wound or in the other case it could be blunt force. Dr. Clark does not provide a description as to where the part of the projectile was found that is described by Dr. Clark [as interpreted]. Case 408T, unidentified person. Dr. Sarajlic says that the injuries were inflicted by at least five projectiles whereas Dr. Clark says that it is at least three projectiles. Case 417T, unidentified person. There is a difference in the number of observed injuries. And then Sarajlic, in paragraph 4 of his opinion, does not rule out the possibility of one more injury in the chest area, which means that Professor Sarajlic says at least four gun-shots wounds, of which three in the head area and at least one in the chest area. Whereas, Dr. Clark says that there are three injuries in the back of the head and two in the chest area. And autopsy number 420T, unidentified corpse. In that case, the difference is as follows. It's in the difference of the direction of the channel of the gun-shot wound. Dr. Clark sees two gun-shot injuries. Dr. Sarajlic thinks that perhaps there were three possible gun-shot wounds to the head. Dr. Clark says entrance wound is in the right back part of the head, and Dr. Sarajlic in the right and central part of the skull. Dr. Sarajlic concludes that it's a gun-shot wound and that metal items were found subcutaneously that resemble projectile fragments, whereas Clark says that three projectile parts were found. If projectile parts were found in the head, then it's a different type of gun-shot wound. There is no entry-exit wound, but only an entry wound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one additional question. If, for example, there's some inconsistency in whether there were two shots to the head or two fragments or three fragments, in how many of these ten cases you just mentioned, would these inconsistency affect the finding? I mean, that if you follow the one, that you come to a different finding as to the cause of death compared to the other one? In how many cases would the inconsistency have such an impact? If you want to further analyse it, I don't require you to immediately answer the question. It's time for a break anyhow, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I would need to analyse the documents in order to be able to draw any conclusions. I focussed only on the differences in the description of the injuries. I did not talk about other inconsistencies that are there. These were just inconsistencies regarding the description of the wounds, there are inconsistencies in the description of the clothing as well as the state of the actual body, and I did not go into those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's time for a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. Mr. Ivetic, could you give us any indication as to where we are at this moment in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was still on track to finish within the seven hours allocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I think, given the estimate that I was given before the beginning of this session, we're still on par to attain that, plus or minus a little bit but not significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which would mean that, in another two hours approximately, you would conclude your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think that's probably right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We take a break, and we resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait until the witness enters the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, now I propose to go through your cases which you highlighted in your Tomasica report under section B. And we have case number 1 appearing on the bottom of the page in Serbian and it will continue onto the next page in Serbian. And, first of all, before I ask you any questions I would like to at this time indicate that given the discussions in court yesterday and the instructions from the Chamber as to these items, we have uploaded the Bosnian autopsy report as disclosed to us by the Office of the Prosecutor for case number 1, which is the footnote 49 in Dr. Stankovic's report as 1D05948 and would then move for it to be admitted alongside the report so the Chamber may have the full information. Unfortunately, we don't have the English translations since those were not provided in the disclosure from the Prosecution, and it -- therefore the -- the -- the -- it should be MFI'd pending translation by the translation unit, since they'll need time to do that. We have -- yeah, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I wonder if I might assist here. Your Honours, the Prosecution has also uploaded them. There was a regrettable lack of communication here, for which I apologise. Our uploads do, in fact, contain English translations so perhaps if we could upload them instead, or rather use them instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. We'll deal with that outside of Your Honours' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, so, Professor, case number 1 which we have on the page, could you tell us what made you determine to highlight this case as an inconsistency in your report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first case indicates an entry wound which, according to Dr. Durmisevic, is in the area of the left parietal bone and according to Dr. Clark, on the left side of the face, whereas the exit wound is in the area of the left parietal bone. Whereas Dr. Durmisevic, let me repeat, claims that it's the entry wound. From a forensic point of view, this is unacceptable, because this raises the question whether the person was hit from the direction of the left parietal bone or whether that's the exit wound. This is the inconsistency that needs to be clarified because on the basis of such a finding, it's not possible to reconstruct the position of the attacker and the victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Professor, we earlier talked about the degree of specificity in the descriptions of the autopsy reports. In relation to this particular case, what comment do you have as to the level of specificity in the injury reports and the findings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case, it follows from the autopsy finding that Dr. Durmisevic -- and as I have a photocopy of his minutes, if I may be allowed to take it and look at the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Stankovic, excuse me, for my ignorance not knowing what the parietal bone is. But I see that according to Dr. Clark, the entry seems to have been on the left side of the face and the exit is also on the left parietal bone. Could there be a typo here or is it possible for the bullet to come through the left side and come out through this left side as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's just possible, just at the left parietal bone means in translation the left back of the head. So in translation once the Latin word is used and the other time it's a translation from the Latin. So that may be the only difference that might be confusing. But the left parietal bone and the left back of the head is one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said you had a photograph, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Photocopy, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's the photocopy of the pathology report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. A photocopy of the pathology report. Is that in evidence yet? Is there any way that we could look over the shoulders of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's just what I was trying to introduce or get an MFI for that my colleague on the other side said that they have uploaded them under their own numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, could you inform us as what to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I wonder if Mr. Ivetic could provide the ERN number for us on that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I think that's 65 ter number 33729. We're just releasing that just now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if there would be any possibility to already give the numbers to the Prosecution for any future --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we -- I think we sent a list yesterday and they should be in the order of the cases. So they're in chronological order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: We'll work on releasing all of them just now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any comment as to the level of specificity as to the descriptions used in the autopsy report that we have before us which was your case number 1 that I highlighted?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the injuries, the report drawn up by Dr. Durmisevic describes the surfaces of fractures and the defects on the bones, and on the basis of that, he made the existing report. Dr. Clark, on page 87, 88 of his summary, also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt for a moment. Is it proper to broadcast this? Because there are names and identification by DNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I discussed that with my colleagues, Your Honour. The names came out through the discussion of the list on the last session and we felt that the names were acceptable. In terms of the identifying characteristics, if they're not going to be discussed, then perhaps it's better not to broadcast these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It seems that Mr. Ivetic does not object to that. Then we'll not broadcast those details, whereas the names are known. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have it back. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, could please continue. You were talking about Dr. Clark, I think, and page 87, 88 in the summary. Could you please continue your answer.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Clark describes in a short way that this is an entry wound to the head with the entry wound probably on the left side of the face where the left eye socket with the surrounding area is damaged. It seems that the exit wound is on the crown of the head on the left parietal bone where there is big damage with edges which are funnel-like opened outwards. So on the basis of this description he concluded and that the direction of the channel is from the left side of the face towards the left part of the crown and ends there. By contrast, Dr. Durmisevic says in item 3 of his opinion, the nature of the injuries to the head corresponds with the impact of a projectile fired from a fire-arm probably from the direction of the left parietal bone towards the back and the exit wound knocking out the squama of the frontal bone. So he does not even link the injuries and does not say that the exit wound is in the left side of the face but he says that it's in the frontal bone, which is the area of the forehead. So that's the inconsistency that can be seen in the findings of these two experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I would ask at this time that we introduce 65 ter number 33729 as the next Defence exhibit number and my question is does this now need to be under seal or ... or maybe provisionally under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we should have it under seal if we want to the details not to become public.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 33729 will be Exhibit D1450, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, under seal. And ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1450, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we could turn to your report, D1447 marked for identification, page 11 in English, page 14 -- page 15 in the Serbian. And at the top above case number 3 we have case number 2, and I wanted to ask you, professor, in relation to the discrepancy between Dr. Durmisevic, on the one hand, and Dr. Clark on the other hand, how significant is the discrepancy of these two pathologists in relation to this particular case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The discrepancy is quite significant because Dr. Durmisevic, in this finding, states, in paragraph 3 of his opinion, the nature of said injuries to the bones of the head, the hips, the trunk and upper extremities corresponds with impact from a fire-arm. And Dr. Clark, on page 12, in his notes on case 042T states that the fractures of the right radius and ulna, that is say, the bones of the right lower arm occurred post-mortem, and the damage to the right fibula, that is the thinner bone in the right lower leg, may have occurred only after death. It is not known on the basis of what parameters Dr. Durmisevic declared that these injuries were sustained while the person was alive and that they were gun-shot injuries and Dr. Clark claims that they occurred after death. Such a discrepancy of opinion is unacceptable from any point of view and would necessitate a harmonisation of positions or, otherwise, a new expert analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask a question, please. Mr. Stankovic, I'm looking at your report, the sentence relating to Dr. Durmisevic. It says: "Autopsy finding describes all injuries as being caused by bullets." I don't see any reference to it being caused before death and it looks like he's just telling us how the injuries were caused by a bullet and Dr. Clark seems not to be talking about how they happened but just talking about the fact that they were occurred on the radius and ulna, and that they occurred post-mortem. It doesn't look like they are talking to the same point here. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Partly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... they were injured and when they were injured. The other one talks about how they were injured.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The autopsy report that I have before me, the full autopsy report signed by Dr. Durmisevic, includes item 4, injuries, where he states where the injuries were registered. Inter alia, he notes or lists the injuries on the body of this specific person Suljo Mujadzic, those that were registered. And he describes the injuries in his report. He says that all the -- all the injuries were caused by gun-shot impacts. He does not say for a single injury that it occurred after death. By contrast, Dr. Clark says that the injuries that I talked about to the bones of the right lower arm and the thinner bone of the right lower leg occurred after death. He does not say at all that they were the consequence of impact of projectiles. He does not describe how they were caused or by what tool they were caused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's precisely the point I'm making. I'm saying the one is talking about how they were killed, how they were shot or injured. They were injured from bullets. That's what Dr. Durmisevic says. On the contrary, Dr. Clark doesn't talk about how they were -- the injuries were inflicted. He talks about where the injuries were inflicted and when they were inflicted. He says that they were inflicted on the radius and ulna and they were inflicted post-mortem. So the two are not talking about the same thing. Therefore, I -- I fail to see how it can be said that they are inconsistent. Because they're describing two different aspects. At least three; one is where and when and the other one is how.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In his report, Dr. Clark notes that the injuries to the head, the multiple injuries to the chest with the fragmentation of the right scapula, the injuries to the hip area and to the right lower leg are gun-shot injuries caused by at least five projectiles but that does not include the injuries to the right lower arm and the right lower leg. So both of them describe gun-shot injuries to the body. But whereas Dr. Durmisevic says that they were caused by projectiles, or bullets, Dr. Clark states that the injuries that I noted, so some of those injuries, may have occurred after death. So what is the truth then? If we are talking about one and the same injuries, the right lower arm and the right lower leg, the thinner bone of the right lower leg, can there be two different opinions about these injuries? Did they occur in lifetime or after death? And what were they caused by, if they were caused after death then it may have been the consequence of burial for some other reason perhaps let me not go into detail but this is a discrepancy that should not exist in autopsy reports relating to one and the same case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It does seem as if you looking also at Dr. Clark's full report before you which I don't have before me. I'm talking about what is written in your report, and what is written in your report, I am still saying, based on that, the topics are different. Dr. Durmisevic talks about the instrument used to injure, whereas Dr. Clark talks about the parts of the body that were injured and that they were injured after death. Dr. Durmisevic doesn't say whether they were injured before or after death. That sentence is silent on when it took place. So to me, it looks like we are comparing apples with oranges here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not mixing anything, Your Honour. You don't have the summary report of Dr. Clark, which categorically talks about the gun-shot injuries that he registered and the injuries that occurred post-mortem. I believe that this is part of Dr. Clark's report and that you must have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But let's now try to be clear. In your last answer you talked about Dr. Clark talking about bullet injuries which I think is not what we find in your summary because there it's about fractures. The only way to resolve the matter is to look at both, the one next to the other, and since the witness does understand some English, I would suggest that we would have both the relevant portion of Dr. Clark's report next to the report of -- of -- of the -- the -- the Bosnian experts and to see to what extent it is, indeed, about the same matters or whether we're talking about different matters. Because I was also struck by the fact that one is talking about bullet injuries and the other one is talking about fractures; whereas I understand from the witness that Dr. Clark also says something about bullet injuries. So, therefore, what we need to fully understand these issues is to have the -- the Clark report next to the other report and then find out what the inconsistency exactly comes down to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My understanding is that Dr. Stankovic has reviewed the B/C/S translation of Dr. Stankovic's chart which is an exhibit in this case so there's a B/C/S translation. He has reviewed the B/C/S autopsy findings of Dr. Durmisevic and Dr. Sarajlic which, now with the assistant of my friends from the Prosecution, I have their numbers and I'm able to offer those for admission into evidence for all of the cases --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- all ten cases. If you want to go through all ten of them, then we would like to have all these detailed reports in evidence and, also to start with, on our screens so that we can compare what the one report says and look at what Dr. Clark tell us about it. That may require some preparation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That may require preparation since I don't have the English translations or even the B/C/S at the time that I had prepared because we were not going to go into that in great detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, we can do two things. To bother about it for the next ten minutes, and see how we can organize it. I think the best way of doing it is that to postpone --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the -- the -- the list of ten reported by Professor Stankovic and then move on perhaps with another subject. But I'd like to come back to the first one, because my question to you would be whatever the differences are on how the damage to the skull is described precisely, is there any disagreement between the experts that the death was caused by the damage to the head of the victim as described in not exactly the same wordings? Do you remember the injury with the parietal bone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Dr. Durmisevic, in his report, notes that the death was a violent one caused by a gun-shot injury to the head. That's paragraph 5 in the said autopsy report. Dr. Clark -- what's the page? - Dr. Clark -- excuse me. Dr. Clark notes that a gun-shot injury to the head, minimum number of shots, one, great velocity hits, and he does not say anything about the cause of death in this section of the report that I have at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you consider it a possibility that with the damage to the head described that someone would survive that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It's just that I believe when I made this observation and when I said the position between the attacker and the victim in the case as cited by Dr. Durmisevic saying that it comes from the left parietal bone, that means that the attacker would be behind and above the victims. This is what I was talking about. I was not talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no, I see that. But my question was about the cause of death, irrespective of whether it came from the left or to the right. But the experts do agree that a gun-shot wound to the head, which you say you couldn't survive, is -- is described by both of them, one explicitly telling us that that's the cause of death, if I understood you well. And I'm talking about the first in the list. Mr. MacDonald, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I'd just like to make sure there is no confusion here. I heard Professor Stankovic say that Dr. Clark says nothing about cause of death in the report he has. I would just like to make sure that Dr. Stankovic is looking at P07444 with that, the long summary list. I just want to make sure that's what he's saying. Otherwise he is [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stankovic may not be familiar with the numbers of documents. But there seems to -- to that extent, no disagreement that Professor Stankovic agrees, whether it's written by Dr. Clark or not, it's an injury which you couldn't survive. And if it's described in that way and if we accept the expertise of both Dr. Clark and Professor Stankovic, then there seems to be no reason to dispute that this caused death or do you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Okay. Then that has been clarified. Before we continue, I have another five minutes. I had not put on the record clearly that 65 ter 33729, I assigned Exhibit D1450 is admitted, under seal. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, with the caveat that we will return to these cases tomorrow, I'd like to ask you if you could summarise for us overall what was the most significant conclusion you had as to the material that you reviewed from the Tomasica investigation, if you had to sum everything up.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my report on Tomasica, by putting questions in a certain way, I also presented certain unclear matters which were presented in the main report as facts, and this is why I wanted to indicate by questions like this that there were many conclusions in the Tomasica report which were not based on the generally accepted forensic medicine positions on conclusion-making, and on the basis of the finding certain conclusions which were verified in the analysis should not have been reached. And this is the question which I was answering throughout my work. I believed that analysis like this or findings such as these ones and differences in the autopsy reports which exists between Dr. Durmisevic, Professor Sarajlic and Dr. Clark had to have been harmonised and then presented to the court in that way. I do not wish to give lessons to anybody, including the Prosecutor. I'm only speaking on the basis of my experience and on the basis of the education that I received and that obliges us to do this. Thus, if there are inconsistencies, and we did discuss this to a certain degree, and I did provide some explanations about that, I said something about that, it's important, then, that all these inconsistencies be looked at by those who drafted the report and they were -- they should have provided a harmonised opinion and harmonised findings, and this is actually what I was trying to get at in my own testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I have to deal with a matter briefly. Therefore, I suggest that we already, at least for today, release the witness. Professor Stankovic, we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, not at 9.30 as usual, but at 9.00, and I inform the parties that there is a chance that the final part may be either 15 bis or that we even adjourn a little bit earlier than usual. Mr. Stankovic, I again instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given. If that's clear to you, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am old enough to be able to understand you very well and to listen to what you are telling me. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that matter I would like to briefly deal with the issue on the -- if I could say the winter or summer clothing, Mr. Ivetic. The transcript was verified, and from what I see here, but it -- a copy will be given to you. Indeed, you made a full quote which includes the line: "... but this was the exception and generally the style of dress would fit with people who had died in the summer months." And then as far as your question is concerned, the question was: "To you what does this multiple layers of clothing indicate? Does it indicate people who had died in the summer months, as Dr. Clark has --" and there it becomes inaudible. From the answer of the witness, I took it that you in one way or another, must have said that Dr. Clark claimed that, or suggested, or whatever, but whether that's the case or not, I do not know. It may well be that the witness also has not heard part of your question or that it was -- I don't know whether it was translated to him. Perhaps we could also listen to the B/C/S audio to see how this was interpreted for Dr. Clark [sic] but at this moment on the basis of the English transcript, it just ends in: "... as Dr. Clark has," and then it stops. The parties should be provided with a copy of this quick verification of the transcript, and I think it might be useful to have the translation in B/C/S verified as well so that we know at least what the witness supposed -- supposedly had heard when he started answering the question, how the B/C/S interpreters have understood what you said in English, which is not reflected in the English transcript. We ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if the parties are preparing anyhow to have kind of a comparative demonstration of what the one report says and what the other report says, it certainly would help the Trial Chamber if you would prepare a hard copy of the ten items so to have both the Dr. Clark and the other -- and the BiH report for us in hard copy, which may save some time in having it before us. Having invited you to do that and to give that to -- to send that to Chamber's staff, we adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 20th of April, 9.00 in the morning.
